story.title: Impeachment Vote Looms for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Amid Political Tensions
story.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing an impeachment vote initiated by Congressman Thomas Massie, who accuses him of conducting military actions against Iran without congressional authorization. Hegseth has criticized the impeachment effort as a political spectacle that undermines U.S. troops. President Donald Trump has expressed his support for Hegseth, vowing to stand by him during this challenging time.

event_overview.title: About Impeachment Proceedings
event_overview.subject: Impeachment Proceedings
event_overview.summary: This event concerns an effort in the U.S. House of Representatives to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth through articles introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie. Impeachment is a constitutional process in which the House may formally charge federal civil officers, while the Senate alone conducts any subsequent trial; it is separate from criminal prosecution.

facts.label: Constitutional authority
facts.value: The U.S. Constitution gives the House the sole power to impeach and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments.

facts.label: Who may be impeached
facts.value: The Constitution makes the President, Vice President, and other civil officers of the United States subject to impeachment for treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors; a Cabinet secretary is a federal civil officer.

facts.label: House and Senate thresholds
facts.value: The House approves articles of impeachment by a simple majority. If articles are transmitted, the Senate considers the case, and conviction requires the concurrence of two-thirds of senators present.

facts.label: Possible consequences
facts.value: A Senate conviction can remove an official from office and may include disqualification from future federal office; it does not bar separate criminal indictment, trial, or punishment.

facts.label: Current House effort
facts.value: On November 9, 2026, Massie presented an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. Reporting described the measure as raising allegations concerning war-powers and other conduct; those allegations are the basis of the proposed articles, not findings of guilt.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the November 9-10, 2026 developments surrounding the proposed House action and Hegseth's response, not a complete account of the underlying allegations, House deliberations, or any possible Senate trial.

explore_lenses.label: What does Massie’s resolution actually allege?
explore_lenses.title: Eight articles reach beyond the Iran war
explore_lenses.summary: The proposal is not limited to one allegation about Iran. The text published by Rep. Thomas Massie sets out eight impeachment articles that accuse Hegseth of unlawful uses of force and other alleged abuses of office.

claims.text: The resolution states that it impeaches Defense Secretary Peter Brian Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors” and presents eight articles to the Senate if adopted by the House.
The first articles allege violations of the War Powers Resolution tied to Iran, including that hostilities lacked congressional authorization and continued beyond the statute’s asserted time limits.
Other articles in the published resolution concern alleged actions involving Venezuela and Yemen, so a vote on the measure would concern a broader set of accusations than the Iran operation alone.

explore_lenses.label: What do Massie and Hegseth argue?
explore_lenses.title: They dispute both legality and consequences
explore_lenses.summary: Massie frames the conduct as unlawful war-making without the required congressional role. Hegseth says the operations were lawful, Congress was notified, and impeachment would harm U.S. military missions.

claims.text: Massie’s resolution argues that the Constitution and the War Powers Resolution limit introducing U.S. forces into hostilities without a declaration of war, statutory authorization, or an attack-created national emergency.

The War Powers Resolution provides for termination within 60 days after a qualifying report is submitted or required, absent a declaration of war, specific authorization, a statutory extension, or Congress being unable to meet; it permits up to 30 additional days for certified military necessity during withdrawal.

Hegseth said the Iran, Venezuela, cartel, and Yemen operations were lawful orders of the commander in chief, were communicated to Congress, and were executed by U.S. forces; he characterized the impeachment push as a political spectacle rather than oversight.
President Trump publicly backed Hegseth, while House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he supported the resolution and accused Hegseth of abusing his position and helping engineer the Iran war.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next procedurally?
explore_lenses.title: The House must act before any Senate trial
explore_lenses.summary: As of November 10, the available House floor record did not show a completed impeachment vote. A House majority would first have to adopt articles; only then would the Senate conduct an impeachment trial, where conviction requires a two-thirds vote.

claims.text: Reuters reporting said the House was preparing a procedural vote on November 10 and that Massie said overcoming that step would allow a debate and vote on the articles.
The House Clerk’s floor summary available on November 10 listed other floor business and a recess, but did not list action on an Hegseth impeachment resolution.

story_report.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie is pushing an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of unauthorized military action, including operations involving Iran. The House was preparing a procedural vote on Nov. 10 that Massie said could lead to debate and a vote on the articles if cleared. President Donald Trump has backed Hegseth, while the available House floor record did not confirm final action on the resolution as of that date.

sections.heading: Massie Resolution Includes Eight Articles
sections.body: Massie’s published resolution would impeach Peter Brian Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors” and, if adopted by the House, present eight articles to the Senate. Its allegations extend beyond Iran: other articles concern purported actions involving Venezuela and Yemen. The resolution’s accusations are allegations rather than findings that the conduct occurred or was unlawful.

sections.heading: War Powers Claims Face Opposition
sections.body: The resolution argues that the Constitution and War Powers Resolution restrict introducing U.S. forces into hostilities without a declaration of war, statutory authorization or an attack-created national emergency. The statute generally requires termination within 60 days after a qualifying report is submitted or required unless specified exceptions apply, with up to 30 additional withdrawal days for certified military necessity. Hegseth has called the operations lawful commander-in-chief orders communicated to Congress and described the impeachment effort as political spectacle; Trump backed him, while House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries supported the resolution.

sections.heading: House and Senate Control Impeachment Process
sections.body: The House holds the sole power to impeach. If it approves articles, it appoints managers to present the case in the Senate, which holds the sole power to try impeachments. Reuters reported that a Senate conviction appeared unlikely because it requires a two-thirds majority, though that was a forecast rather than a vote result.

unresolved.text: The final House disposition of Massie’s resolution, and any eventual Senate vote, were not confirmed in the floor record consulted as of Nov. 10, 2026.
The supplied materials do not provide a judicial or congressional finding resolving whether the alleged operations violated the War Powers Resolution.
